Record note: All three students are charged, not convicted. The posts described here are allegations from charging documents and news reports.

Three University of South Alabama students were arrested on Friday, October 2, 2026, and charged federally with threatening the president — over three separate social-media posts made in the days before Donald Trump's rally at the school's Mitchell Center in Mobile, Alabama.

The three posts

The posts were unconnected. Amare Jemal Woods, 18, a freshman, posted a TikTok on September 27 saying “he gotta die bro.” Cameron Lamark Lewis, a philosophy major, posted twice on X on September 26 — one invoking Utah Valley University (“remember the University of South Alabama the same way they remember Utah Valley University” — where Charlie Kirk was assassinated on September 10, 2025) and one referencing rapper BloodHound Q50. Kayla Leaann Smith posted a TikTok on September 29 saying “We only got one chance let’s take it” alongside an image mimicking holding a gun. NY Post · People

How they were found

The FBI surfaced the posts through social-media checks run ahead of Trump's visit, then identified the posters through emergency disclosure requests and university police. Mobile County Sheriff Paul Burch assisted in monitoring the students. The cases were unsealed Friday afternoon; all three were detained over the weekend, with detention hearings set for Monday, October 5. Fox News

The university draws a line

The Mitchell Center rally was not university-sponsored — the venue was rented by the Republican National Committee — and the university condemned the threats. The rally went ahead as planned; Trump told the crowd, “It sort of all began here.”

The other side

None of the three has been convicted; the charges are allegations. Woods’s attorney Jason Darley described his client as “a very young, very small kid” — “the furthest away from any defendant I’ve ever represented in federal court in 21 years” — and framed the post as “a comment made in jest, and in poor taste has been taken seriously by the federal government.” People

Hochul appoints AG James as special prosecutor

Governor Hochul issued an executive order appointing Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor, removing the criminal investigation from Tompkins County DA Matthew Van Houten — saying ‘newly released information’ had undercut public faith in the DA’s investigation.

The Chi Phi national chapter said on September 30 that three days after Jane Doe’s October 2024 police report, the Xi chapter voted unanimously to remove the accused members; the national council then permanently expelled them. The Cornell Xi chapter was shut down in 2024 and remains barred.

DA Van Houten told CBS New York he was never given the transcript of Jane Doe’s November 14, 2024 campus-police interview: ‘I’m going to follow up on this because this is news to me.’ The #IAmJaneDoe movement is rallying to protect Jane Doe’s identity (Mashable).

October 1, 2026

Newly released texts: Jane Doe's messages with one of the alleged attackers

Verified X account Bridget Ayers (@BridgetAyers, 3.9M views) published text-message transcripts obtained by ABC News between Jane Doe and one of the alleged Chi Phi attackers. In October 23, 2024 texts, Doe says “everyone knows,” her “reputation is destroyed and i’m utterly ashamed,” and it’s “RUINING my life temporarily.” On November 7, the fraternity member says his ex told him he’s “being labeled as an assaulter” and asks if she said something; Doe says she never mentioned his name. On November 8 — the same day she filed her complaint — Doe writes “i think i’m done talking to you. i know you lied.” Ayers’ read: the texts show fallout from campus gossip and embarrassment rather than discussion of a rape — “the clearer it becomes why prosecutors may have declined to bring charges.” ABC’s own writeup confirms the same exchanges.

September 28, 2026

DA publishes full statement on the 2024 no-charges decision; reopens case for grand jury

Tompkins County DA Matthew Van Houten published a detailed written statement explaining why his office declined criminal charges in November 2024.

According to the DA, Jane Doe’s six-page sworn statement — with 20+ handwritten notations, signed under penalty of false statement — “did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped” and instead “described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual.”

The DA writes that neither Jane Doe nor her attorneys contacted his office in the nearly two years since; he reached out to her attorneys after the civil lawsuit was filed to address the discrepancy.

His legal analysis concludes the statement, taken as true, could not sustain charges under NY Penal Law 130.05: no alleged forcible compulsion, no drug administered without consent, no alleged unconsciousness — and per the statement, each time she asked to stop, the conduct stopped.

“did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped”
— DA Matthew Van Houten, Sept 28 statement

The DA called the fraternity members’ behavior “disgusting and morally reprehensible” but said prosecutions must rest on evidence.

He has reopened the investigation and assigned a senior sex-crimes prosecutor to prepare the case for presentation to the Tompkins County grand jury, which can consider Jane Doe’s testimony and the civil complaint’s allegations.

Tompkins County — DA statement (Sept 28, 2026) ↗

On the night of October 19–20, 2024, a 20-year-old Cornell student alleges she was gang-raped by seven Chi Phi fraternity brothers at the fraternity house in Ithaca, New York. She told campus police weeks later that she was "with 100% confidence" raped. The district attorney says he never saw that transcript — and now the case that was declined in 2024 is reopening.

The night she alleges

According to the 101-page civil lawsuit filed in mid-September 2026 — most outlets report September 16, the New York Post dates it September 18 — Jane Doe visited a friend at the Chi Phi house while already intoxicated. Two fraternity members allegedly pressured her into taking what they said was ketamine, and the assaults allegedly continued until 5:45 a.m. Around 1:42 a.m., one member allegedly posted a degrading "free p----" message in the "Chi Phi Actives" Snapchat group; a later exchange allegedly read "Shop still open?" / "Yea." The lawsuit names Cornell University, the seven men, the fraternity, an Ithaca bar, and others — alleging breach of contract, negligence, and violations of state law, seeking unspecified compensatory and punitive damages. She has since dropped out of Cornell. Newsmax · CBS News

"With 100% confidence I was raped"

On November 14–15, 2024, she sat for a two-day interview with Cornell campus police — a Title IX investigator, a victim advocate, and partly her adviser. The investigator read her account back to her word by word for corrections. She drew a line between what she says she consented to early on — "Yeah, as much as I can be because, again, I was super drunk when I got there ... But I was pretty OK with all of this" — and what she says followed: "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped... I'm very confident about this." She recalled "multiple men" coming in while she was naked, being "totally disgusted," and being "the most intoxicated I've ever been in my life... unable to make any decisions." NY Post

The six-page statement and the DA's decision

That interview was distilled into a six-page sworn statement, which she made more than 20 handwritten corrections to before signing. Tompkins County DA Matthew Van Houten declined charges in 2024, saying the statement "did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped" — it "described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual." The Sun

The missing transcript

Van Houten now says his office never got the full transcript: "I never saw it, never heard it until tonight... If she had said those words, we certainly would want to have explored that more." Cornell campus police say "all investigatory information" was shared. Cornell's Tuesday FAQ says the DA also received the Snapchat screenshot; Van Houten told ABC News he never received that either — calling it a "critical piece of evidence." Ithaca city police say the incident was never reported to them. Cornell says it supports reopening the case. In a contentious CNN interview this week, anchor Jake Tapper pressed Van Houten on the non-prosecution; the DA said he was "constrained by the law" and that the fraternity members' text messages weren't in the original police report. Inside Higher Ed · CNN via YouTube

The case reopens

On September 28, 2026, the DA reopened the criminal investigation and said he plans to present evidence to a grand jury — telling CBS's Lilia Luciano he hopes to get it before the grand jury within the next 45 days. The grand jury can consider the charges set out in the civil complaint plus others. Her attorney Thomas Giuffra called it "a step in the right direction, albeit a late one" — and added: "Not one of these guys was arrested. Not one." Two days later, Governor Kathy Hochul said she had spoken with Cornell President Michael I. Kotlikoff and that Cornell agreed to hire outside counsel for an independent investigation. Senator Charles Schumer called for "a truly independent and exhaustive investigation — not only into what happened, but into how this case was handled." CBS New York · Newsmax

Two tracks of punishment

While the criminal case stalled, Cornell ran a parallel multi-month Title IX investigation. At a September 29 student government meeting, President Kotlikoff detailed the sanctions: two of the seven were expelled, two suspended for at least two semesters, one had already graduated before punishment, and two were found not responsible for sexual misconduct. Cornell stated that "none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence" and that "any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false." The Chi Phi chapter itself was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus. The national fraternity moved even faster: interim executive director Trey Robb said that three days after Doe's police report, the Xi chapter voted unanimously to remove the accused from the rolls, and the national Grand Council permanently expelled them — "These actions went beyond anything the law or Cornell University required of us." Chi Phi nationally partners with RAINN. CBS News · Inside Higher Ed

The other side speaks

Two of the accused have been named. Scott Kretzchmar's attorney Jeremy Saland says Kretzchmar allegedly sent two responses in the Snapchat group, but calls the messages inappropriate rather than evidence of assault — saying Kretzchmar briefly entered the room, did not touch her "in any way, shape or form," and left within minutes; Cornell found him not responsible, and a hair follicle test showed no ketamine in his system. Gillio Lopes's attorney Andrew Miltenberg says Lopes "unequivocally denies the allegations." No criminal charges have ever been filed against anyone. CBS News

The texts

Two days after the night, Doe texted one of the brothers. He apologized "for how things went down," said his memory was "kinda fuzzy," and felt bad they were too intoxicated to "shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand." She replied that her memory was "super clouded too," that "non(e) of the sexual stuff was illegal," said she liked being with him and another man, and suggested smoking together again "but like leave out the extra 5 billion men and ketamine." Her attorney Giuffra confirmed she texted a defendant shortly after but could not confirm those specific texts, attributing her tone to denial and trauma. YouTube

Status hearing: dismissal motions filed, November 2 arguments set

Lindsay Clancy spoke in court for the first time since the mistrial — “Good morning” to the judge. Her lawyer Kevin Reddington filed motions to dismiss on double-jeopardy grounds, sought an investigation into holdout juror Michael Desronvil, and claimed a “total and complete lack of evidence” she killed her children — even though she formally stipulated during trial that she strangled them. Judge Sullivan ruled on nothing; arguments on the dismissal bid are set for November 2. She remains on suicide watch at a state psychiatric hospital.

New York Post — hearing updates ↗ Reuters — returns to court ↗ People — Clancy speaks in court ↗ CBS News (Instagram) ↗

Coming up

  1. November 2, 2026Arguments on Reddington’s motion to dismiss the case (double-jeopardy bid) before Judge Sullivan in Plymouth County Superior Court.

On January 24, 2023, Lindsay Clancy strangled her three young children with exercise bands in the family basement — then tried to take her own life. She has never disputed killing them. The entire fight, three and a half years later, is over whether she was criminally responsible — and one holdout juror kept it alive. Wikipedia

The 11–1 deadlock

The trial began July 20, 2026 in Plymouth County Superior Court before Judge William Sullivan and ran about six weeks. Deliberations started August 27; after roughly 38 hours over seven days, the jury deadlocked 11–1 — eleven for not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility, holdout juror Michael Desronvil favoring conviction. A mistrial was declared September 4, 2026. Reuters · Reuters

The September 29 hearing

At the status hearing, Reddington filed motions to dismiss plus a required finding of not guilty (the double-jeopardy argument), and sought an investigation into Desronvil — his juror-questionnaire answers and alleged cellphone use during deliberations. The judge ruled on nothing; dismissal arguments are set for November 2. DA Timothy Cruz’s office has said nothing about a retrial; options include a plea deal or retrying on lesser second-degree murder charges, which would let her waive a jury for a bench trial. Reddington said June 2027 is his soonest availability. NY Post · People

“Good morning” — and a claim that stunned the courtroom

Clancy spoke in court for the first time since the mistrial: “Good morning.” Then Reddington claimed a “total and complete lack of evidence” she killed her children — even though she formally stipulated during trial that she strangled them. She remains on suicide watch at a state psychiatric hospital. People · NY Post

The defense: postpartum psychosis

The defense case was postpartum psychosis and bipolar disorder — no criminal responsibility. In the months after Callan’s birth she repeatedly sought treatment from multiple providers and hospitals for insomnia, intrusive thoughts, and suicidal ideation. The prosecution’s answer: she was in control — she sent her husband Patrick out beforehand on an errand (collect medication and dinner), she reported the commanding voice only on the day of the killings, and no clinician ever observed psychosis. Wikipedia

The Trump/pardon thread

Days after the mistrial, Reddington asked Trump for a pardon on Good Morning America. Trump punted — a “state situation” (presidents can’t pardon state charges) — and said in the Oval Office: “she did a horrible, horrible thing. Can’t be worse… There’ll be a price. It’s going to be mental institution or jail or something.” At the September 29 hearing, Reddington said attacks on Clancy come “from politicians, from President Trump, all the way down.” Rep. Nancy Mace separately called for a “public execution.” The Daily BS · Reuters

Patrick’s second act

Ex-husband Patrick Clancy remarried — Dr. Rachel Danis, a fertility doctor — in April 2026. In their first joint interview, around September 20 on 60 Minutes with Ross Douthat, Patrick described waking up screaming and said EMDR therapy worked “like a miracle”; the couple confirmed they’re expecting a child (Douthat confirmed the pregnancy on CBS Mornings). Patrick was the prosecution’s first witness, testifying for two days. He blasted the conspiracy theories accusing him: “deeply harmful to the legacy of my children.” Parade · NY Post · People

The holdout speaks

Desronvil went on Hannity after the mistrial: “the whole focus has been on me, but we want to reel everything back and put the focus on the three angels.” Mandatory

October 1, 2026 — Brief published: the science on sexual orientation

The Trump House brief on the science of sexual orientation is live — covering the half-million-person GWAS that found no “gay gene,” the twin studies, the fraternal birth-order effect, prenatal hormones, and Lisa Diamond’s research on sexual fluidity. Medical Xpress — 2019 GWAS

The slogan is “born this way.” The science is more complicated — and more interesting. The largest genetic study ever conducted found no “gay gene.” Twin studies say genes explain only part of the picture. And the strongest evidence that orientation is set before birth comes not from genes, but from the womb itself. Medical Xpress · PNAS

The “gay gene” that wasn’t

In 2019, Ganna et al. published a genome-wide association study in Science covering about 477,522 people — the largest ever on same-sex behavior. The result: no “gay gene.” Five genetic loci with tiny individual effects, together explaining less than 1% of the variation; all genetic variation combined, just 8–25%. You cannot predict a person’s orientation from their DNA. Medical Xpress · GEN

What twins tell us

Identical twins share sexual orientation more often than fraternal twins — but not reliably. A 2008 study of 3,826 twin pairs estimated genetics accounted for about 35% of the variation in men and 18% in women, with roughly 64% coming from non-shared environment. Same DNA, often different orientations: genes matter, but they don’t decide. ScienceDaily

The womb: the fraternal birth-order effect

Each older biological brother raises a man’s odds of same-sex orientation by about a third. Adopted and stepbrothers don’t count — but biological brothers raised apart still do, pointing to the prenatal environment, not upbringing. A 2017 study linked elevated maternal antibodies to NLGN4Y, a Y-chromosome-linked brain protein, and researchers estimate the effect may account for orientation in 14.8–48% of gay men. Wikipedia · PNAS

Prenatal hormones

The INAH-3 region of the hypothalamus correlates with orientation, and natural experiments point the same way: people with congenital adrenal hyperplasia (exposed to extra prenatal androgens) and people with androgen insensitivity show shifted patterns of attraction — evidence that prenatal hormone exposure helps shape orientation. PNAS review

The fluidity wrinkle

Psychologist Lisa Diamond’s research shows “born this way” doesn’t account for sexual fluidity — especially in women, whose attractions can shift over the lifespan. That complicates “fixed and immutable” without supporting “choice.” Nobody in the research literature treats orientation as something people pick. Diamond’s talk

The history

In 1973 the APA removed homosexuality from the DSM. In 1993 came the famous Xq28 “gay gene” claim — which was never replicated; a 1999 replication attempt failed. The field has moved on: the modern picture is genes plus womb plus environment, with no single cause. The APA’s own position is that there is no scientific consensus on what causes sexual orientation — “nature and nurture both play complex roles.” Xq28 review (PDF) · APA position paper (PDF)

September 30, 2026 — Execution fails: Pike survives two doses of pentobarbital

On September 30, 2026, Tennessee attempted to execute Christa Pike, 50, by lethal injection at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. She survived TWO doses of pentobarbital — her lawyers said she had not lost consciousness, still had a heartbeat, and was “audibly snoring.” She was taken by ambulance to a nearby hospital; her condition is unknown. New York Post

Tennessee's protocol calls for a secondary set of syringes “if the inmate is not deceased” after the first dose — it does not say what happens if she is alive after the second. Governor Bill Lee ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review” and halted the remaining scheduled executions for the rest of the year: “the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective.” Robin Maher of the Death Penalty Information Center called what Pike experienced “singular and unparalleled.” New York Post

Tennessee set Christa Pike's execution for 10 a.m. CDT on September 30. An hour before it was scheduled, the Sixth Circuit stayed it. That evening the U.S. Supreme Court lifted the stay 6–3, with Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissenting; Sotomayor called the Court's intervention “stunning.” The state proceeded — but after two doses of pentobarbital, Pike remained alive. USA Today · New York Post

The night the protocol failed

Just before 7:30 p.m. CDT, Pike was strapped to the gurney. WKRN reporter Tori Gessner heard her say, “My arm feels like it's about to bust. One spot is really throbbing.” Her final statement, reported by the AP's Kim Chandler, was: “I'm at peace. I'm ready to be free... This is a happy day.” At 8:53 p.m., media witnesses were escorted out. Pike was then taken by ambulance to a nearby hospital. The Tennessean · New York Post

The execution was intended to make Pike the first woman executed in Tennessee in 206 years and the 19th woman put to death in the United States since capital punishment resumed in 1976. CNN · PrimeTimer

The murder of Colleen Slemmer

On January 12, 1995, Pike, 18; Tadaryl Shipp, 17; and Shadolla Peterson, 18, lured 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer from the Knoxville Job Corps Center to the University of Tennessee's agricultural campus. Prosecutors said the attack lasted 30 to 60 minutes. Slemmer was beaten, her head slammed into concrete, and her throat repeatedly slashed with a box cutter; a meat cleaver and chunks of asphalt were also used. A pentagram was carved into her chest while she was alive. USA Today · LegalClarity

Pike kept a piece of Slemmer's skull as a souvenir, showed it to students, and bragged about the killing. A UT grounds worker found Slemmer's body the next morning and initially mistook it for an animal. Prosecutors said Pike's motive was jealousy over Shipp. Wikipedia · PrimeTimer

Conviction, death row, and clemency

A jury convicted Pike in March 1996 and sentenced her to death at age 20. Shipp received life imprisonment; Peterson received probation after testifying for the state. The Tennessee Supreme Court unanimously upheld Pike's conviction and sentence on October 5, 1998. In 2001, Pike tried to strangle fellow inmate Patricia Jones with a shoestring. Wikipedia · LegalClarity

Pike's clemency case argued that jurors never heard evidence of childhood rapes, PTSD, brain damage, and bipolar disorder. A state attorney answered: “The standard is not a painless execution. Psychological harm alone is not a violation.” Amnesty International and more than 100 women's advocacy groups sought a reprieve. CNN · USA Today

Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, said before the execution attempt: “I just want Christa down so I can end it... There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Colleen.” USA Today

This is a viral-allegations-and-denial story, not a finding. No outlet cited here has independently authenticated the alleged profiles, account records, email attribution, or login data.

Verified facts

September 30, 2026 — Clubhouse room poll: Do humans share common ancestry with chimpanzees?

Matt's Clubhouse room ran a live poll tonight: 'Do humans share common ancestry with chimpanzees?' Results from 123 votes — Yes, we do: 54% · No, we do not: 27% · I honestly have no idea: 12% · Dismiss poll: 9%.

Scientific consensus on evolution is overwhelming. Public belief is far more divided, and the century-old fight over what belongs in science classrooms is active again in state legislatures and federal court.

The scientific consensus

Among scientists, evolution is foundational biology rather than a live scientific controversy. Pew Research Center found near-unanimity among members of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, even as the broader public remained sharply split.

  • 98% of AAAS scientists say humans and other living things have evolved over time.
The divide is not merely between science and faith; it is also about what Americans mean when they hear the word evolution.

What Americans say

Americans do not divide into only two camps. Some reject human evolution, some accept it as guided by God, and some accept it without a divine role. The answer changes substantially with the wording of the question.

  • 37% of Americans say God created humans in their present form within the last 10,000 years.
  • 34% say humans evolved, with God guiding the process.
  • 22% said humans evolved with no divine part in Gallup's 2019 poll — a record high.
  • Only 39% said they “believe in the theory of evolution” in 2009.

Accuracy note

The most recent Gallup figures above are cited via an Answers in Genesis summary (September 2026); polling on evolution is sensitive to question wording.

Why the classroom keeps becoming the battleground

For more than a century, the central legal question has shifted. The Scopes era criminalized teaching evolution. Later cases struck down bans and “balanced treatment” mandates. In 2005, Kitzmiller v. Dover found that intelligent design was a religious view, not science, and could not be presented as a scientific alternative in a public-school biology class.

The recurring argument is not whether schools teach biology, but whether law can require a religious alternative to be taught as science.

The fight returns in 2026

Oklahoma SB 1868 was filed in January, and similar measures surfaced in Colorado, Missouri, and Montana. In September, a federal courtroom in Atlanta again took up Cobb County's evolution disclaimer stickers — another dispute over whether singling out evolution for special skepticism crosses a constitutional line.

Videos

The landmark public debate, the Scopes trial, and the Dover intelligent-design case in full context.

Timeline

  1. 1859Charles Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species.
  2. 1925Scopes trial, Dayton, Tennessee: teaching evolution itself is the crime.
  3. 1968Epperson v. Arkansas: the Supreme Court voids bans on teaching evolution.
  4. 1987Edwards v. Aguillard: the Supreme Court kills “balanced treatment.”
  5. 2005Kitzmiller v. Dover: intelligent design is ruled creationism in a lab coat, not science — “breathtaking inanity,” from a Republican churchgoing judge.
  6. 2014Bill Nye and Ken Ham debate at the Creation Museum; roughly 3 million people watch live.
  7. January 2026Oklahoma SB 1868 is filed; similar bills surface in Colorado, Missouri, and Montana.
  8. September 2026The Cobb County disclaimer-sticker case returns to federal court in Atlanta.

Accuracy note: The IRGC letter urges Americans to vote against President Trump and Republicans. It does not literally name the Democratic Party; Jonathan Turley's “Vote Democratic” phrasing is editorial extrapolation.

On September 29, 2026, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps — a U.S.-designated terrorist organization — published a 25-page open letter addressed to “the honorable people of the United States,” urging Americans to reject President Trump and Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections.

The message from Tehran

Published in English and Farsi, the letter targets American scholars, students, and journalists. It urges voters to punish Trump and the GOP in the midterms, oppose U.S. support for Israel, and “take back control.”

At a Tehran press conference, IRGC spokesman Brig. Gen. Hossein Mohebbi called Trump “an inveterate liar” motivated only by wealth. He said Americans were “not knowledgeable about many developments” and would “think differently and take other decisions” if they were.

“an inveterate liar”

The letter's claims — and the record

The IRGC claims there is not “a single verifiable instance where the IRGC has committed an act of violence against civilians.” That arrives as Iran's regime is accused of killing between 7,000 and 30,000 protesters during its January crackdown. The letter blames Trump and Israel for the war and claims high fuel prices are decimating the U.S. economy.

Constitutional-law professor Jonathan Turley amplified the story at 2:29 AM on September 30. His post drew roughly 436,000 views, 13,600 likes, and 6,200 reposts.

“It is not a good sign when the IRGC shifts from ‘Death to America’ to ‘Vote Democratic.’”
  • 25-page letter addressed directly to “the honorable people of the United States.”
  • 7,000–30,000 protesters killed in the regime's January crackdown, according to accusations cited in reporting.
  • ~436K views · 13.6K likes · 6.2K reposts on Turley's September 30 post.

The Michigan Senate connection

Abdul El-Sayed is the Democratic nominee for Michigan's open U.S. Senate seat, which Gary Peters is leaving. El-Sayed won the August 4 primary with 48.5% and faces Trump-endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on November 3.

At the University of Michigan's September 23 “Students vs. Billionaires” town hall, Iranian-American student Iman Dashti said his cousin “was hunted in the streets of Iran by the IRGC because her hijab wasn't on right,” and that his uncle was sentenced to death and given 50 lashes. Asked to condemn the IRGC and regime directly, El-Sayed instead said the United States should not be “the world's policeman.”

Leaked audio from a private campaign call on March 1 — one day after Ayatollah Ali Khamenei's death — captured El-Sayed saying:

“There are a lot of people in Dearborn who are sad today, so, like, I just don't want to comment on Khamenei at all.”

Khamenei was killed February 28 in joint U.S.-Israeli airstrikes on Tehran. Iranian state media confirmed his death the next day, and his son Mojtaba was appointed supreme leader on March 8.

September 29, 2026 — Phone-evidence reversal: Crump's own expert walks it back, DA fires back

Andrew Garrett (Garrett Discovery), the digital forensics expert on Ben Crump's own team who examined Nolan Wells' phone, clarified he never meant to suggest someone else accessed the phone after Wells' death. DA Angel Myers McIlrath (Jackson County) responded in a Thursday press release: Crump's team never provided the full digital download — only two emails with ~300 pages of selected findings. She says neither the state autopsy nor Dr. Roger Mitchell's independent autopsy found fatal injury, neither ruled out drowning, and: “The Crump team advised my office that they had no evidence of a crime against Nolan Wells.” McIlrath: “If the Crump team genuinely has new information or evidence that Nolan Wells was murdered they should stop playing games and immediately provide it to me.” Crump's team has not responded to Mississippi Free Press requests for comment (September 25 plus four follow-ups). Context: the September 21 grand jury returned no true bill, but there is no statute of limitations on homicide in Mississippi — credible new evidence could re-present the case.

Record note: Nolan Wells was 18. Nobody has been charged in his death. The friends named here were cleared by a Jackson County grand jury and are not accused of wrongdoing in this brief. Claims are attributed to the outlet or document they came from; where accounts conflict, both are shown. This is a record of reported facts and claims, not an opinion.

Nolan Xavier Wells, 18, disappeared during a July 4 boat trip to Horn Island; his body was found in the water two days later, and both autopsies leave his cause and manner of death undetermined.

Follow the Triton — July 4, 2026

Nine stops reconstructed from the Garmin GPSMAP track in MDMR Marine Patrol report MP2607-0016. All times are Central Time; narrative positions are approximate where the report does not give a coordinate.

  1. 19:56 AMLeaves the dockThe white 2000 Triton MI4088BU departs a private dock on El Camino Real Road for Horn Island with about seven people aboard.
  2. 211:14 AMThe west tipThe vessel anchors at 30°14.603′N, 088°46.427′W, among a gathering of roughly 300 people; GPS shows it stationary from about 11:15 AM to 4:30 PM.
  3. 3~4:00 PMBilge-pump failureA Sea Tow caller says the bilge pump stopped working, the boat is taking on water and everyone aboard is accounted for. The request is later canceled; Sea Tow does not respond.
  4. 44:31 PMLeaves without NolanThe Triton heads north at 0.06–4.2 knots for about 2.75 miles. Another friend's boat reportedly tows it. Nolan is not aboard; his phone is.
  5. 55:25 PMBack up to speedThe track returns to normal operating speed, about 30–35 knots.
  6. 65:44 PMBack at the dockThe vessel arrives again at El Camino Real Road.
  7. 75:52–6:06 PMFourteen minutes into Fort BayouThe Triton heads east into Fort Bayou and returns. The purpose of this short trip has not been publicly explained.
  8. 86:36 PMThe loopThe boat travels southwest to Saint Martin Bayou, southeast to the Biloxi Bay Bridge, then north toward Fort Bayou Boat Launch.
  9. 97:19 PMFort Bayou Boat LaunchThe vessel arrives at the launch, is trailered to Cardinal Lane by 7:47 PM and records its last GPS point at 7:59 PM. The family's phone examiner places Nolan's phone at a residence around 7:30 PM.

Source: MDMR Marine Patrol report MP2607-0016 · The named friends were cleared by the grand jury; nobody has been charged in Wells' death.

What the record establishes

A Jackson County grand jury unanimously returned a no true bill after hearing from 43 witnesses under 132 subpoenas. DA Angel Myers McIlrath said investigators found no credible evidence of criminal conduct and “not a scintilla of evidence” that Wells’ death was racially motivated.

The grand jury did not close the door forever. Its report says the matter should return if credible evidence later points to a non-accidental death.

“If credible evidence comes to light in the future that suggests Mr. Wells’ death was non-accidental, this matter should be represented to the Jackson County Grand Jury for further consideration.”

The unresolved medical gap

The state examiner described the body as consistent with drowning, but neither the state chief medical examiner nor the family’s pathologist, Dr. Roger Mitchell Jr., certified drowning as the cause. Mitchell’s report says there was no water in Wells’ lungs, airway, or stomach and documents acute blunt-force injuries to the head and body before death.

Those injuries are real; what caused them and whether they prove foul play remain unknown. The state autopsy documented two scalp contusions, no skull fracture, and no fatal head injury.

Same body. Same phone. Two readings.

The state and the family's experts rely on much of the same physical and digital record but emphasize different conclusions and unanswered questions.

Cause
State & grand jury

Cause and manner undetermined; the position, condition, timing and location were consistent with drowning as a diagnosis of exclusion.

Family's team

Also undetermined; the family stresses the state report's finding of no water in the lungs, throat or stomach.

Head bruises
State & grand jury

Two roughly two-inch scalp contusions, no fracture and no fatal injury; the grand-jury report connected the bruising to a witnessed slip around 3:30 PM.

Family's team

No white-blood-cell response indicated injury shortly before death; the family asks what caused the recent blunt-force trauma.

Phone
State & grand jury

The grand jury reviewed a 261-page Snapchat report and 21-page device exam. The DA says deletions were user actions by other Snapchat users, not physical access to Nolan's phone.

Family's team

Andrew Garrett says the phone stayed on the boat, was last touched around 2:18 PM and contained 282 pages of recovered deleted Snapchat content; he could not say who deleted it or why.

Leaving
State & grand jury

The grand jury found Nolan chose to stay on the island while the phones returned on the boats.

Family's team

His parents say staying behind was out of character; a reported secondhand sighting around 6 PM has not been confirmed by an official source.

Next step
State & grand jury

The case can return to a grand jury if credible new evidence points to a non-accidental death.

Family's team

The CBC, NAACP and Ben Crump have asked DOJ and the FBI for an independent federal review; no public response has been reported.

“Elmore and I do not believe that Nolan simply and accidentally drowned, and nobody saw anything, and no one knows anything.” — Christine Wonsley, Wells’ mother
  • 23 grand jurors: 12 white, 5 Black, 2 Hispanic, 2 Native American, 1 Asian, and 1 listed as “other.”
  • 132 subpoenas and 43 witnesses preceded the unanimous no true bill.
  • 282 pages covering about 300 Snapchat messages were included in the phone extraction.

What changed this weekend

On September 26, hundreds gathered at Government and State streets in Ocean Springs to honor Wells and demand transparency; members of the Black Hebrew Israelite group Israel United in Christ marched through the demonstration. Ocean Springs resident Jeron Lowery, who knew and had employed Wells, remembered him as a respectful young man.

The next day, reporting carried the DA’s explanation that other users had deleted or unsent their own Snapchat messages and that the activity did not show someone accessing Wells’ phone.

A viral “restored final words” recording is not Wells speaking from his phone. It is a 37-second Sea Tow distress call about a boat taking on water off Horn Island; a forensic expert said the enhanced audio could not be verified, and an attorney called it doctored.

The Chicago Crusader’s Inner City News has grouped Wells, Tasia Fortune, and a Maryland hanging-suicide under a “Lynchings By Suicide” frame. That framing is an interpretation, not a finding in the Wells case.

The federal threat cases — a separate track

These cases concern alleged threats to a witness's family and a judge connected to the Wells case. They are not charges in Nolan Wells' death.

Edward James Porter

Porter, 32, of Berwyn, Illinois, is accused of threatening Bart Edmiston Jr.'s family. He pleaded not guilty; trial is set for October 5 in Gulfport before Judge Taylor McNeel.

Joseph Alfredo Vasquez Dumarce

Dumarce, 27, of Sacramento, is accused of sending a Facebook bomb threat to Chancery Judge Ashlee Cole. Trial is set for November 2 in Gulfport before Judge Sul Ozerden.

Michelle Francine Edwards

Edwards, of Cincinnati, is accused in a criminal complaint of making 21 threatening blocked-number calls to a chancery clerk's office and the Jackson County Sheriff's Office.

Brandon Ephraim Washington

Washington, of Jacksonville, Florida, is accused of threatening Bart Edmiston Jr. and his father. A publicly confirmed trial date was not identified in the reviewed record.

  • Around October 1 · Atlanta — tentative Crump news conference with Dr. Roger A. Mitchell Jr. on both autopsies.
  • October 5 · Gulfport — U.S. v. Edward James Porter trial.
  • November 2 · Gulfport — U.S. v. Joseph Alfredo Vasquez Dumarce trial.

The friends' side

The grand jury cleared the named friends. Their lawyers say public accusations damaged innocent people and are pursuing a separate defamation track.

Cleared by the grand jury

Warren Hudson, Jax Pitalo, Morgan Seymour and the other friends named in the public record were not charged. The unanimous no true bill said allegations against the boats' occupants were not based in truth.

Cease-and-desist notices

Lawyers for Hudson, Pitalo and Seymour sent Sunny Hostin and ABC's The View a cease-and-desist on September 16 demanding a retraction and apology within 10 days. An intent-to-sue letter went to Rev. Al Sharpton on August 21.

Defense fund

Hudson, Pitalo and Seymour launched a GiveSendGo legal-defense fund that had passed $90,000 by August 3.

What is filed

As of September 27, no reported defamation suit had been filed. The public record described notices and threatened litigation, not a judgment.

A separate case — do not merge them

Wells was not hanged. De’Martravion “Trey” Reed, 21, was found hanging on the Delta State campus on September 15, 2025, and that death was ruled a suicide. Reed’s death is a separate case with different facts.

“We will not confuse the absence of an indictment with the presence of an answer.” — Rev. Al Sharpton

Key quotes from the record

Seventeen attributed statements from the state record, the family, investigators, advocates and the friends' representatives.

“There is absolutely no evidence to support the allegations that Nolan's disappearance and death were racially motivated. Nolan's friends loved Nolan and Nolan loved them.”Grand Jury Report · September 21
“The allegations against the occupants of the Triton, the Palm Beach, and the Tideline are not based in truth, and are solely the result of public clamor and private malice.”Grand Jury Report · September 21
“Nolan chose to stay on the island that day, and there is not a scintilla of evidence to contradict that.”Grand Jury Report · September 21
“There was bruising on the back of Mr. Wells' head, which was not a fatal injury.”Grand Jury Report · September 21
“He saw Wells slip awkwardly off the side of a boat around the time of 3:30 p.m. on July 4, 2026, but could not say whether Mr. Wells struck his head during the fall.”A witness, as summarized in the Grand Jury Report
“The Crump team knew better, but did not do better.”DA Angel Myers McIlrath · September 21
“If the Crump team genuinely has new information or evidence that Nolan Wells was murdered they should stop playing games and immediately provide it to me.”DA Angel Myers McIlrath · September 24
“The user action discussed by Mr. Garrett is from other Snapchat users, not someone physically accessing Nolan Wells' phone.”DA Angel Myers McIlrath · September 24
“There were things that were deleted from the phone.”Andrew Garrett, Garrett Discovery · September 24
“The grand jury left us with questions. Nolan's family deserves answers. What caused recent blunt force trauma to his head?”Ben Crump · September 22
“Last night was a reminder that our son's life does not matter to those who hold positions that are supposed to serve and protect the public.”Christine Wonsley · September 22
“There was never any evidence of a crime. Suggestions otherwise were always pure fabrications.”Bart Edmiston Jr., through attorney Russell Latino · September 22
“You should apologize immediately to completely innocent young men Warren Hudson, Jax Pitalo, and Morgan Seymour.”Edward Andrew Paltzik, attorney for the friends · September 22
“Hey we're at the west tip of Horn, and our bilge pump stopped working. We're sinking.”Sea Tow caller · around 4:00 PM, July 4
“The world is watching, and Nolan Wells' family deserves a thorough accounting of what happened.”Derrick Johnson, NAACP · August 19
“If it was your child, you would want the investigation to stay open and active.”Kristen Clarke, NAACP · September 22
“No True Bill Does Not Resolve How Nolan Wells Died.”Ben Crump · September 21

Verified facts

  • Wells, an Ocean Springs resident and freshman wide receiver at Southwest Mississippi Community College, went to Horn Island with a large group on July 4 and was last seen around 3 p.m. His body was found off the island’s northwest shore on July 6.
  • Both autopsies list cause and manner as undetermined. The state autopsy records two dark red-purple scalp contusions of roughly two inches, no water in the airways, and no skull fractures.
  • Mitchell reported acute blunt-force injuries to the head and body before death, with trauma occurring within the first hours. He said the record does not establish whether Wells entered the water voluntarily or was forced and that the investigation should remain open and active.
  • The grand jury unanimously returned a no true bill after 132 subpoenas and 43 witnesses. It expressly allowed re-presentation if credible new evidence points to a non-accidental death.
  • The phone review produced 282 pages covering about 300 Snapchat messages. McIlrath says other users deleted or unsent their own messages; an attorney for three friends says they never possessed Wells’ phone.
  • The Congressional Black Caucus requested an independent federal review on August 12. Crump renewed that request September 22 and 24; no DOJ response has been reported.
  • Hundreds demonstrated in Ocean Springs on September 26. Members of the Black Hebrew Israelite group Israel United in Christ marched, and resident Jeron Lowery — who knew and had employed Wells — remembered him as a respectful young man.
  • The viral “final words” tape is the Sea Tow distress call, not an audio recording from Wells’ phone.
  • Four people — Edward James Porter, Joseph Alfredo Vasquez Dumarce, Michelle Francine Edwards, and Brandon Ephraim Washington — face allegations tied to threats against a witness's family, a judge, or public offices. Those are separate cases; none is charged in Wells' death.
  • The named friends were cleared by the grand jury. Their lawyers sent defamation notices to Sunny Hostin and ABC's The View on September 16 and to Rev. Al Sharpton on August 21; a GiveSendGo defense fund had raised more than $90,000 by August 3.

Timeline

  1. July 4, 2026Wells travels with a large group by boat to Horn Island; last seen around 3 p.m.; a boat reportedly takes on water.

  9. September 24Crump releases the full independent autopsy details and the 282-page Snapchat count.

Verified: The disappearance and recovery dates; the unanimous no true bill; the 132 subpoenas and 43 witnesses; both autopsies’ undetermined findings; the documented scalp contusions; Mitchell’s blunt-force findings; the phone-page count; the DA’s deletion explanation; the re-presentation clause; the September 26 demonstration; and the debunked tape. Disputed or unresolved: Whether the injuries prove foul play, whether deleted messages conceal wrongdoing, whether race affected the death or its handling, and whether the file is effectively closed.

Clarion Ledger — Third suspect gets bond at September 28 hearing

On August 3, 2026, Tasia Fortune, 29, was found hanging from a tree behind a vacant home in West Jackson, Mississippi.

The reaction

The image — a Black woman hanging from a tree in Mississippi — immediately drew claims of a modern-day lynching. Rep. Ayanna Pressley led roughly 60 Democrats in a September 8 letter to the Attorney General and FBI demanding a federal probe into “modern-day lynchings,” citing 10 hanging deaths of Black Americans in 2026; AOC and Pressley posted it on X September 10.

What investigators say

But investigators now say Fortune was killed in a drug dispute before her body was hung in a staged scene — and all three men charged with her murder are Black.

  • Of the 10 deaths cited in the letter, only Fortune’s is an active homicide case.

Verified facts

  • Fortune, 29, a mother of four, was found August 3 hanging from a tree at the 500 block of Road of Remembrance in West Jackson. The medical examiner ruled her death a homicide; Jackson police Det. Samuel Dukes testified September 25 that the scene and hanging were “staged.”
  • Dukes said Fortune was likely dead two to three days before she was found. He testified that she was killed in a drug dispute, with “missing illegal narcotics” central to the crime, and that she fought hard with her attackers.
  • Three Black men have been arrested on murder charges: Jarques “Jock” Ratliff, 51, arrested September 11, pleaded not guilty September 14 and held without bond; Earnest Lloyd Jr., 25, arrested September 22, pleaded not guilty and denied bond; and Eric Clark, 45, who turned himself in September 25 and had an initial appearance scheduled for September 28.
  • A court affidavit says “a black cable cord” was used to hang Fortune from the tree.
  • Hearing testimony described Ratliff and Fortune as friends who were “intimate with each other”; Ratliff also blurted out in court that they were friends. His attorney says he was not involved.
  • The September 25 hearing is to determine whether Ratliff’s case goes to a grand jury. It resumes September 30 at 2 p.m., with portions closed to the public.
  • Pressley’s September 8 letter went to Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel. It was co-signed by roughly 57–60 Democrats, including AOC and Congressional Black Caucus chair Yvette Clarke, and invoked the Emmett Till Antilynching Act.
  • AOC and Pressley posted the letter on X September 10, framing the deaths as “widespread modern-day lynchings” and “racial terror.”
  • Of the 10 hanging deaths cited in the letter, only Fortune’s is an active homicide investigation. One North Carolina case is suspicious and remains open; the rest were ruled suicides.
  • The Associated Press corrected its own reporting: the original “staged lynching” wording was changed to a “staged” scene. Police never said the staging was meant to mimic a lynching.
  • Fortune’s mother, Christy Spivey, said she knew her daughter died before the hanging, “but that step brought all the attention to it.” She added: “What bothered me was they said Tasia fought for her life. I know she did. I know my daughter.”
  • JPD Chief RaShall Brackney said September 25 that the Robbery-Homicide Division “will continue its investigation until all individuals believed to be involved are held accountable.”

Timeline

  1. August 3Fortune is found hanging in West Jackson.
  2. September 8Pressley sends a letter to the Attorney General and FBI.
  3. September 10AOC and Pressley post the letter on X.
  4. September 11Ratliff is arrested on a murder charge.
  5. September 14Ratliff pleads not guilty and is denied bond.
  6. September 22Lloyd is arrested on a murder charge.
  7. September 23Lloyd pleads not guilty and is denied bond.
  8. September 25Dukes testifies that the hanging was “staged” and describes a drug dispute; Clark turns himself in and is charged with murder; the hearing is recessed to September 30.
  9. September 28 · ScheduledClark’s initial appearance.
  10. September 30 · ScheduledRatliff’s hearing resumes, with portions closed to the public.

3 Students, 3 Threats, 1 Rally: The South Alabama Trump Threat Cases · Host talking points

  1. Open with the speed: three separate posts, three separate students, zero coordination between them — and all three are in federal custody within days. The FBI was already watching social media ahead of the rally, which means the net was cast before a single post went live.
  2. The campus-free-speech fault line: Woods's lawyer calls it "a comment made in jest, and in poor taste" taken seriously by the feds. Lewis's lawyer calls it political speech protected by the First Amendment. Ask the room: is "he gotta die bro" on TikTok a threat or a meme? And does the answer change when the president is in town?
  3. The Utah Valley University line is the prosecutor's strongest exhibit. Lewis didn't just vent — he invoked the place where Charlie Kirk was assassinated three weeks earlier. That's the post that turns a campus edgelord into a federal case in the government's telling.
  4. Contrast the fates: the rally went ahead anyway, the RNC rented the building, the university condemned the posts. The machine doesn't stop for three students. Ask the room whether the deterrent effect is real or whether it just teaches the next kid to post anonymously.
  5. The Monday hearings are the next chapter: all three detained over the weekend, detention hearings Monday October 5. The brief updates the moment there's a ruling — that's the hook to bring the room back.
  6. Clubhouse-ready: "Three students. Three separate posts. Zero coordination. All in federal custody before the weekend was over. Where's the line between an edgy post and a federal crime — and who gets to draw it?"

The Cornell 7: "100% Confident I Was Raped!" · Host talking points

  1. The missing transcript: campus cops recorded her saying "with 100% confidence I was raped." The DA says nobody gave him the transcript — he worked off a six-page summary she corrected 20+ times. Cornell says it shared everything. Somebody's file was incomplete, and that gap decided whether charges were filed.
  2. The consent arc: she admits the night started consensually. Her own interview draws the line between "pretty OK with all of this" and "completely and totally incapacitated." That distinction is either her strongest evidence or the defense's best exhibit — depending on who's talking.
  3. The texts: two days later she wrote the sex "wasn't illegal" and wanted to hang out again. Her lawyer calls it trauma denial; a jury will call it reasonable doubt. Denial is a documented trauma response — but it's also a defense attorney's dream.
  4. The punishment menu: no arrests ever — two expelled, two suspended, one already graduated, two cleared. Meanwhile the fraternity itself moved faster than the DA: a unanimous vote to cut the accused three days after her report. Cornell's parallel justice is its own scandal.
  5. The grand jury gamble: the DA is reopening on the same police file plus a lawsuit. What changed legally? Nothing new was found. What changed politically? Everything. Ask the room: is this new evidence, or new pressure?
  6. Clubhouse-ready: "She said it to campus cops in 2024 — 'with 100% confidence I was raped.' The DA says the transcript never reached his desk. If the words were in the file all along, who failed her — the campus police, or the prosecutor?"

11-to-1: The Mistrial, the Holdout Juror, and the Fight Over Lindsay Clancy's Retrial · Host talking points

  1. The 11–1 split is the show: eleven jurors were ready to acquit on lack of criminal responsibility, and one man — Michael Desronvil — hung it, then went on Hannity. One holdout against eleven: that's the room's opening question.
  2. The defense's whiplash: she stipulated at trial that she strangled them, and now Reddington claims a “total and complete lack of evidence.” That's not confusion — it's retrial positioning. Name it as strategy.
  3. Postpartum psychosis is on trial: she sought help from multiple providers and hospitals for months — the system knew. The prosecution says sending Patrick out on the errand proves planning. Ask the room which fact wins.
  4. The Trump/pardon thread: her lawyer asked Trump for a pardon on GMA, Trump punted, and now the lawyer says attacks come “from President Trump, all the way down” — plus Nancy Mace calling for a “public execution.” The case is a political football now.
  5. Patrick's second act: remarried, expecting a baby, 60 Minutes, EMDR “like a miracle” — and the internet conspiracy sleuths accusing him anyway. Grief vs. the internet: “deeply harmful to the legacy of my children.”
  6. Clubhouse-ready: “If eleven jurors say she wasn't criminally responsible, should one holdout keep this alive? What does ‘justice’ look like when the defendant is paralyzed and on suicide watch?”

Born This Way? What the Science Actually Says About Being Gay · Host talking points

  1. Slogan vs. science: “born this way” was a political and legal strategy — immutability helped win court cases. The science is messier. Know the difference between the slogan and the studies.
  2. The strongest “born” evidence is the womb, not genes: the birth-order effect works in brothers raised apart, and maternal antibodies are a prenatal mechanism. That is very hard to square with “choice.”
  3. The identical-twin problem for strict “born this way”: same DNA, often different orientations. If it were purely inborn and genetic, twins would match every time.
  4. The fluidity wrinkle: women’s sexuality shifts more over the lifespan. That complicates “fixed and immutable” without supporting “choice” either — hold both halves at once.
  5. The honest frame: “not a choice” and “born this way” are different claims. The science strongly supports the first; the second is an oversimplification. Say the true thing.
  6. Clubhouse-ready: “If science found a ‘gay gene’ tomorrow, would it change anyone’s mind about rights? What if it proved the opposite?” Then ask what the rights argument actually rests on.

She Survived Her Own Execution: The Botched Lethal Injection of Christa Pike · Host talking points

  1. The state tried to kill her twice in one night and she lived — "snoring" on the gurney. DPIC calls it "singular and unparalleled." That's the story.
  2. The legal whiplash: Sixth Circuit stay an hour before, SCOTUS 6-3 overrule, then the protocol itself failed. The system moved heaven and earth to execute her tonight — and the drugs didn't work.
  3. The Eighth Amendment question is now live, not theoretical: her lawyers filed emergency motions mid-execution citing "unnecessary agony."
  4. Don't lose Colleen Slemmer: the 30–60 minute torture, the pentagram, the skull fragment shown to classmates. Her mother waited 31 years and watched tonight end in chaos.
  5. The mitigation the jury never heard — childhood rapes, PTSD, brain damage, bipolar — vs. the state's "psychological harm alone is not a violation." That's the whole clemency debate in one line.
  6. Clubhouse-ready: "What happens now?" The protocol has no provision for surviving the second set, and Lee paused all executions for the year. Does Tennessee try again?

Candace Owens Denies Viral Lesbian Dating Profile Claims · Host talking points

  1. The denial did not address the specific items her critics keep citing — the alleged URI.edu email, the claimed “Candamo429” link to a 2008 YouTube channel, and the birthday-based portmanteau. Those details remain allegations, not authenticated evidence.
  2. The hypocrisy angle writes itself: she built a brand accusing others — including Brigitte Macron, Taylor Swift, Eminem, Nick Fuentes, and Erika Kirk — of hidden sexuality, and now she is getting the same treatment.
  3. Her response was “most deranged,” followed by blaming Zionists and the “Epstein class” without evidence. Critics will call that deflection; the fair question is what specific evidence she disputes and what she can disprove.
  4. The entire cheating claim rests on one alleged login timestamp from 2022. A login does not prove who logged in, why, or that any encounter happened, and IBTimes could not authenticate the underlying record.
  5. Even Nick Fuentes — “I don't want to attack her on the lesbian thing — it's irrelevant” — and Bilyeu's team flag this as unverified rumor. The honest read: this story is about her brand, not her bedroom.
  6. Clubhouse-ready: “Does a tradwife brand survive a data-breach OSINT thread?” Then ask what would actually prove or disprove the allegation. One possible move would be to subpoena FriendFinder for access logs.

South Carolina Mom Charged in 50-Stab Attack on Her Own Kids · Host talking points

  1. The system had her: February 2024 child-endangerment charges still pending, out on bond — and the kids stayed with her. “No prior criminal history” (no convictions) vs. pending charges — the charged-but-not-convicted gap is where kids fall through.
  2. The detail that breaks a room: a hungry 6-year-old's phone call is what exposed 50 stab wounds. Grandma + the ex-boyfriend were the safety net that worked.
  3. “Visions,” rapid speech, fleeing the stretcher — mental-health crisis, criminal accountability, or both? Ask the room where the line is.
  4. 50 wounds, cut to the bone, possible amputation — charged with attempted murder. The law-and-order question practically asks itself.
  5. Neighbor to WSPA: “I'm just praying that [the children] are placed somewhere that they will be safe and taken care of” — the community's verdict on the system that left them there.

Do You Believe in the Theory of Evolution? · Host talking points

  1. The gap is the show: 98% of scientists vs. a public where only ~1 in 3 think Darwin's theory is well-supported by evidence. Ask the room why — and watch it split along faith lines, not education lines.
  2. Seven in 10 Americans see God's hand in human origins. This isn't a science-literacy story, it's a who-do-you-trust story — and that's a better room.
  3. It's live right now: four states plus a federal courtroom in Atlanta are relitigating what kids learn about where they came from. “What should your kid be taught?” is the call-in angle.
  4. Disarm the “activist judges” rebuttal in advance: the Dover judge was a Republican churchgoer who called the ID policy “breathtaking inanity.”
  5. Make both sides answer the same question: “What evidence would change your mind?” — the answers will tell you everything about the room.

IRGC to America: Vote Trump Out · Host talking points

  1. A U.S.-designated terrorist organization is now openly campaigning in an American election — and its message is word-for-word the Democratic platform: dump Trump, abandon Israel, “take back control.”
  2. The IRGC letter reads like DNC talking points with a Tehran dateline. When the world's worst terrorists and one American party want the same election outcome, that's the room's opening question.
  3. El-Sayed won't condemn the IRGC; the IRGC wants his party to win. He calibrated his silence on a dead terrorist for Dearborn votes — connect those dots out loud.
  4. Michigan decides Senate control. The IRGC's preferred outcome is a Democratic Senate, and their ideological ally is leading the polls there.
  5. Anticipate the pushback: “The letter doesn't name Democrats.” True — and the honest version hits harder: Iran wants the party less likely to hold them accountable. That's exactly why Turley's framing lands.
  6. The Dearborn quote is the kill shot: “There are a lot of people in Dearborn who are sad today” — a U.S. Senate candidate mourning a terrorist's death with his voting bloc, on tape.

Nolan Wells · Host talking points

  1. The “deleted messages” bombshell just deflated — Crump's own expert says nobody else touched the phone.
  2. DA vs. Crump credibility fight: she claims they privately told her office they had no evidence of a crime while publicly demanding answers.
  3. Who controls the evidence: 300 selected pages vs. the full download.
  4. The door isn't closed: no statute of limitations means this can come back.
  5. “Undetermined is not exoneration — and it’s not a murder finding either.” Both pathologists agree on exactly one thing: they do not know how Nolan Wells died. The grand jury found no crime; the family found no answers. Anyone on air who turns “undetermined” into a verdict in either direction is lying about what the documents say. The honest sentence is the shortest: nobody knows how he died.
  6. “The injuries are real, the cause is not.” Two dark red-purple contusions under the scalp, inflicted within hours of death — both autopsies document them, and nobody has explained them. That is the family’s strongest fact and the DA’s weakest moment. But “unexplained” is not “homicide”: the same reports found no skull fracture, no fatal injury, and no water in the airway. Hold both halves at once.
  7. “The DA’s most explosive claim got the least attention.” McIlrath says the family’s own lawyers told her office last month that their investigation found no evidence of crimes while publicly demanding the case stay open. If true, that is a devastating detail for the cover-up narrative. Ask it as a question on air: what did the family’s investigators find, and why has Crump not addressed it?
  8. “The ‘final words’ tape was fake — and that matters for credibility.” A viral clip sold as Nolan’s restored last words was actually a Sea Tow distress call about a sinking boat, and a forensic expert says the enhanced version cannot be verified. Every fake artifact that circulates makes the real unanswered questions easier to dismiss. Debunk it on air — it protects the legitimate questions.
  9. “The grand jury left the door open — use that.” The report itself says credible evidence of non-accidental death should be re-presented. That is not a cover-up document; it is an invitation. The pressure point is not the September verdict, but the pending full phone analysis and whether the DA keeps the file genuinely active.
  10. “Two cases, two standards — don’t merge them.” Wells drowned-or-didn’t in open water with undetermined autopsies; Trey Reed was found hanging on a college campus and ruled a suicide within days. The Crusader is now bundling them into one “Lynchings By Suicide” narrative. Conflating them is exactly the error we owned before — keep them surgically separate or lose the audience’s trust.

Honesty guardrail: “We will not say Nolan Wells was murdered — no one has been charged, the grand jury found no crime, and both autopsies say undetermined. We will not say he simply drowned — neither pathologist would certify that either. What we’ll say is what’s on paper: an 18-year-old with unexplained head injuries, a phone with deleted messages, and a cause of death nobody can name. The family deserves the file opened, not a verdict invented.”

The Tasia Fortune Case · Host talking points

  1. The flagship "lynching" now has three Black murder suspects and a drug motive — missing narcotics, a victim "intimate" with the accused, statements "you would only know if you were there," a black cable cord. Nothing in the court record says "hate crime."
  2. Even the AP had to correct itself — police never said the scene was meant to look like a lynching. The narrative outran the sworn testimony within 24 hours. Stick to what was said under oath.
  3. Scoreboard: 9 suicides, 1 drug murder with Black suspects, 1 open case. And the DOJ/FBI's answer has been total silence — no probe announced. Silence from Patel's FBI is itself the story.
  4. Humanize what D.C. flattened: foster-care kid, gifted athlete, four little kids, starting a cleaning business — killed in a drug dispute, then hung up for reasons nobody will explain. Her mother says it was personal, and the staging "brought all the attention to it." The people who made her a "racial terror" talking point haven't revisited the story since Friday.
  5. Watch the next two dates: Clark's initial appearance Monday (Sept 28), Ratliff's hearing resuming Wednesday (Sept 30, partially closed). Every hearing buries the lynching frame deeper.
  6. Honesty guardrail, updated: "Police have not said the staging was meant to mimic a lynching, and neither will we. What they did say, under oath, is that Tasia Fortune was murdered in a drug dispute and hung from a tree two to three days after she died. That's damning enough — and it's more than the letter's authors have acknowledged."
